sources.title: Avelino (2018; online 2017), Mexico City Spanish
sources.locator: pp.223–229; vowel inventory and stress pp.227–228
sources.whatItSupports: Five vowel phonemes; stress, contextual variation, and the selected Mexico City reference variety.
sources.limitations: Descriptive six-speaker illustration, not an L2-training intervention. It supports the inventory, not the effectiveness or full lexical IPA of this draft.

sources.title: Fox, Flege & Munro (1995), The perception of English and Spanish vowels by native English and Spanish listeners
sources.locator: Methods pp.2541–2543; dissimilarity task and MDS results
sources.whatItSupports: Cross-language perception of Spanish /i e a/ among English monolingual and Spanish–English bilingual listeners.
sources.limitations: Dissimilarity-rating study, not Spanish HVPT or efficacy evidence. Spanish stressed CV syllables were excised from words; the full words below are not its administered stimuli. No /o u/ results from this experiment are claimed.

sources.title: Pérez Silva (2017), La adquisición de oposiciones en bilingües castellano–quechua y quechua–castellano
sources.locator: Discussion of vowel inventories and acquisition, Figures 3–10
sources.whatItSupports: Explains why the Spanish mid/high split can require a new distinction for some Quechua-background learners.
sources.limitations: Theoretical analysis discussing prior production/perception work; not an independent validation of these words or a Mexican-Spanish training trial. Quechua varieties and bilingual experience differ.

contrasts.scopeNote: One member of the complete ten-comparison grid for five vowels. This grid is inventory coverage, not ten equally difficult or equally research-supported lessons.
contextNotes: Target only the stressed vowel of the first syllable. Every candidate is a disyllable with an open first syllable; spelling and meaning are review metadata.
Two groups match the unstressed final vowel: final /a/ and final /o/. Each group has three lexical items in each category; keep A/B/X in the same group to avoid a category-correlated final-vowel cue.

targetSegment names the category and targetOccurrence=1 selects its first occurrence, including repeated vowels in casa, masa, pala, polo, tomo and mono. A later occurrence or opposing vowel is not the target.
Consonantal frames still vary. Group balance removes one obvious nuisance cue, not every coarticulatory or lexical confound; actual item/talker validation is still needed.
reviewNotes: All entries are drafts for human text review. Dictionary checking confirms these are real words and selected senses; it does not certify the editorial IPA or any audio.
Pools are independent category banks; row alignment does not assert minimal pairing. Only minimalPairs lists single-segment substitutions under the selected broad IPA. An empty list is intentional.
No words are tagged as published experiment stimuli. Even pato, named as a source word by Fox et al., supplied an excised CV rather than a whole-word stimulus.
ABX is the intended product interaction, not an intervention proven superior by these citations. Research and pronunciation validation must not be inferred from inventory completeness.

gaps: Integration note: es-e-i is a deeper replacement for the earlier two-word-per-category draft. The other nine IDs are new comparisons. Deduplicate by ID when merging; do not count es-e-i twice.
Ten is the full set of binary comparisons among five vowel categories, not a claim that Spanish has only ten useful sound contrasts or that every comparison is equally difficult.
No audio is approved or generated. All word IPA remains subject to human review; newly linked dictionaries were checked for headwords and senses, not full displayed IPA.

Reference variety is Mexico City. Its seseo means /s–θ/ is not a contrast here; distinción needs a separate variety bank. Yeísmo means ll/y is not a universal opposition. Written b/v must not become a Mexican /b–v/ lesson.

Mexico City voiced-stop lenition and unstressed vowel reduction occur naturally. Broad /b d ɡ/ labels do not demand stop realizations between vowels; tubo/cubo and dedo require consistent natural allophony. The target vowel stays stressed in this pack.
Consonant coverage remains incomplete: review useful /f/, /s/, /x/, /tʃ/, /l/, nasal and rhotic comparisons against particular learners and dialects. This bounded pass closes the vowel-grid gap only.
Connected-speech vowel sequences, hiatus/diphthongs, unstressed-vowel variation and additional stress contexts require separate pools; they are not silently treated as isolated monophthong contrasts.
This small inventory is reused across comparisons. It is not 120 independent lexical items, and the words cannot simultaneously serve as unseen transfer-assessment items.

L1-specific priority still needs diagnostic validation. The cited English-listener study used ratings, not Spanish training; the Quechua discussion is not uniform evidence for every bilingual speaker.
